chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Amr ibn Abi al-Miqdam, who said:

I saw Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) on the Day of Arafaat at the Mawqif, and he was calling out in a loud voice: 'O people! The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was the Imam, then Ali ibn Abi Talib, then al-Hasan, then al-Husayn, then Ali ibn al-Husayn, then Muhammad ibn Ali (peace be upon him), then Hah!' So he called out three times to those in front of him, and on his right, and on his left, and behind him, making twelve calls in total.

So they said: 'Hah' in the language of the clan of so-and-so means 'I', so ask me.' He said: 'Then I asked others as well from the masters of Arabic, and they said the same.'
ai.seo_question: Who are the twelve Imams mentioned by Imam al-Sadiq at Mawqif?
ai.summary: This hadith, recorded in Al-Kafi, highlights the Imam's public declaration of the Twelve Imams' succession during the pivotal Day of Arafaat, a time of spiritual convergence for pilgrims. The use of the dialectal term 'Hah' for 'I' serves as a linguistic marker for the twelfth Imam, emphasizing the continuity of divine authority (Imamah) from the Prophet through the Ahl al-Bayt. This narration underscores the Shia belief in the explicit designation (Nass) of each Imam by his predecessor, reinforcing the theological legitimacy of the Imams' leadership.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Muhammad Bin Al Husayn, from Al nazar Bin Suweyd, from Amro Bin Abu Al Miqdam who said, 
‘I saw Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> of the Day of Arafaat by the Pausing Station, and he<sup>asws</sup> was calling out in a loud voice of his<sup>asws</sup>: ‘O you people! Rasool-Allah<sup>saww</sup> was an Imam<sup>saww</sup>, then Ali<sup>asws</sup> Bin Abu Talib<sup>asws</sup> was an Imam<sup>asws</sup>, then Al-Hassan<sup>asws</sup>, then Al-Husayn<sup>asws</sup>, then Ali<sup>asws</sup> Bin Al-Husayn<sup>asws</sup>, then Muhammad<sup>asws</sup> Bin Ali<sup>asws</sup>, then Hah!’ So he<sup>asws</sup> called out three times to the ones in front of him<sup>asws</sup>, and on his<sup>asws</sup> right, and on his<sup>asws</sup> left, and for (those who were) behind him<sup>asws</sup>, being twelve calls (in total).
And Amro said, ‘So when I went to Mina, I asked the masters of Arabic about the interpretation of (the word) ‘Ha’.
So they said, ‘Ha’ in the language of the clan of so and so (means), ‘I, therefore ask me’. Then I asked others as well from the masters of the Arabic, and they (all) said similar to that’.
en.sarwar: 10. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from al-Nadr ibn al-Suwayd from ‘Amr ibn abu al-Miqdam who has said the following:

“I saw abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, on the day of ‘Arafah in al-Mawqaf (the station) saying at the top of his voice, ‘O people, the Messenger of Allah, O Allah, grant compensation to Muhammad and his family worthy of their services to Your cause, was an Imam. Then Ali ibn abu Talib was an Imam. Then al-Hassan was an Imam. Then al-Husayn was an Imam. Then Ali ibn al-Husayn was an Imam. Then Muhammad ibn Ali was an Imam. Then, Hah.’ He then called three times toward his front, right, left and backside; twelve voices.’
I (the narrator) then went to Mina and asked Arab linguists about the meaning of the word “Hah.”
They said, ‘It is an expression of banu so and so, meaning, “I am the one. Ask me whatever you want.” I then asked other Arab linguists and they also said the same thing.”
